stages.name: Labour market failure and intervention
stages.title: Labour market failure and intervention
stages.sub: Why immobile labour and weak wage-setting justify government policy, and how to judge that policy.

steps.q: A factory in Newcastle needs welders but the unemployed workers nearby only know retail skills, and cannot afford to move to where welding jobs are. Do these workers fill the vacancies?
steps.right: No, the jobs stay unfilled and workers stay unemployed
steps.wrong: Yes, they retrain and move straightaway
steps.hint: Think about what stops someone taking a job they are not skilled for or cannot move to.
steps.pre: So skills mismatches and inability to move leave

steps.q: Workers are sitting unemployed while firms elsewhere cannot find staff, purely because people cannot switch jobs or move. Is the market putting labour where it is needed?
steps.right: No, resources are not being used efficiently
steps.wrong: Yes, it sorts itself out through wages
steps.hint: If workers and vacancies never match up, is the market working well?

steps.q: A single large employer in a small town is the only one hiring cleaners, and pays them less than cleaners earn elsewhere. Left alone, will the market fix this low pay?
steps.right: No, the employer can keep paying below the competitive wage
steps.wrong: Yes, competition between employers will push pay up
steps.hint: With only one buyer of labour, what stops pay from rising on its own?

steps.q: Vacancies stay empty and workers stay jobless because of skills mismatches and immobility. Would fixing this let the economy produce more and cut unemployment?
steps.right: Yes, matching workers to jobs raises output and cuts unemployment
steps.wrong: No, total output would stay exactly the same either way
steps.hint: If idle workers could fill the empty vacancies, what happens to what the economy produces?

steps.q: The retail workers near Newcastle lack welding skills. What kind of scheme would let them take the welding jobs on offer?
steps.right: A government-funded course teaching them welding skills
steps.wrong: A grant to help them move house closer to the jobs
steps.hint: Their problem is skills, not location. What fixes a skills gap?

steps.q: The training course costs the government money now, but the workers will not be job-ready for a year, and some may drop out or not use the new skills. What must be weighed before judging the policy a success?
steps.right: Its cost, delay and how many workers actually benefit
steps.wrong: Only whether the course exists at all
steps.hint: Spending money is not the same as the policy working well straightaway.
